title: Activate Industry!: Moving Beyond Defense to Disruption and Active Defense

segments.text: >> ANNOUNCER: Please welcome, Vice President,
Google Threat Intelligence, Google Security, Sandra Joyce.
>> SANDRA JOYCE: Thank you, RSA Conference.
It's an honor to be back.
Over the last decade, we have built a global community
of defenders that's more connected and mature than ever.
Public-private collaboration has moved from a rare occurrence
to a daily operational reality.
This has given us unprecedented levels of shared
visibility into the threats that we are facing.
But while we celebrate this foundation, we have to
recognize a fundamental shift in our role.
We are now in a position where we can
and we must actively shape the outcome of adversary behaviors.
We have to step up because the adversaries that we face
are not standing still.
Our opponents are resilient.
They are well-resourced.
They are backed by sophisticated ecosystems
of contractors and intelligence services.
We see this in the shift towards mass extortion groups
like FIN11, who use zero days to exploit hundreds
of organizations simultaneously.
The actors behind BRICKSTORM were specifically
targeting enterprise suppliers to harvest data
for zero-day deployment and downstream pivots.
Now, for several years, we have monitored
the trend of threat actors specializing in
phases of ransomware and extortion operations.
So in 2025, the shift became statistically significant
within our dataset.
In our just-released 2026 M-Trends report, we found that
the median time between initial access and the handoff
to the secondary threat group has dropped from eight hours
in 2022 to just 22 seconds in 2025.
Now, what this means in practice is that
we are seeing a shift from opportunistic selling
to pre-planned partnerships.
Rather than a threat actor gaining access and looking for
a buyer, your criminal groups are now coordinating handovers
before the initial breach even occurs.
Now, this evolution highlights a significant
increase in the organization, coordination, and ultimately
the sophistication of the cybercrime ecosystem.
And as the clock winds down to seconds, the stakes are
only getting higher.
Adversaries are increasingly embracing AI, which is changing
the landscape in three important ways.
The first is speed.
The speed of attacks enabled by agentic AI will
break security operations that rely on human intervention.
Agentic approaches for exploit development will allow
adversaries to outpace human-driven controls.
Second is scale.
Adversaries are scaling global operations by leveraging agentic
AI and open-source frameworks like HexStrike MCP
to automate the full attack lifecycle.
We have seen actors like APT31 use these tools and agentic
workflows to test attacks against targets
here in the United States.
The third is sophistication.
Threat actors are leveraging AI to significantly improve
existing capabilities and uplift activity across the
entire intrusion lifecycle.
This will put major capabilities like access to
zero days into the hands of well-resourced threat actors.
Now, for a decade, we have been saying intelligence
sharing is key.
But intelligence sharing alone is not sufficient.
We have to do more.
With threat actors increasingly turning to AI,
there is a newfound urgency for defenders to go upstream
and disrupt at the source.
The private sector operates the very infrastructure
that adversaries abuse.
And this gives us a unique vantage point and
the technical capabilities that government agencies
sometimes don't have.
And disrupting threat actors must become the
status quo in our industry.
We must move towards a philosophy of active defense.
Now, to be clear, this is not hacking back.
This is the legal and ethical use of intelligence to protect
our own platforms.
Our goal is to shift the economics of the entire
ecosystem to make cyber threat operations so costly,
so difficult, so risky that it's no longer a viable
path for any adversary.
Now, by bringing together the right partners,
we can create comprehensive disruption that sticks.
At Google, we are focused on complex,
high-impact operations that meaningfully degrade and disrupt
serious threat actors.
Now, our disruption strategy is built on
four specific pillars.
First is civil legal action.
We rely on legal action to hold threat actors
accountable and seize the infrastructure they rely on.
Second is public disclosure.
We use sunlight as disinfectant to burn attacker
tools and force them into costly retooling phases.
The third is technical takedowns.
We create a hostile environment for attackers on
our platforms and those of our partners.
And fourth is product hardening, which
often overlooked, but perhaps the most crucial.
We are not just kicking bad guys off the platform;
we are driving product improvements and remediation
to prevent them from ever getting back in.
So let's examine how this looks in practice.
I'm going to tell you about some of the disruption work
we have been doing, like with IPIDEA.
IPIDEA's proxy infrastructure is a little-known component of
the digital ecosystem that's leveraged by a wide
array of bad actors.
In contrast to other types of proxies, residential proxy
networks sell the ability to route traffic through IP
addresses owned by internet service providers
that service residential or small business customers.
So by routing traffic through an array of consumer devices
all around the world, attackers can mask their
malicious activity by hijacking those IP addresses.
We actually observe distillation attacks on our
AI models using the IPIDEA infrastructure.
So this creates a massive blind spot for defenders.
Specifically, IPIDEA promotes three critical risks.
IPIDEA has become notorious for its role in
facilitating several botnets.
Their software development kits, or the SDKs, are a primary
engine for building and controlling botnets.
We saw this with BADBOX 2.0 last year, and more recently
with the Aisuru and Kimwolf botnets.
It turns innocent users into exit nodes.
So by hijacking residential IPs as launchpads for crime,
it can cause unsuspecting consumers to be flagged
or blocked by their own providers.
These applications effectively punch holes in home networks.
Once a device becomes an exit node, bad actors can pivot to
any other private device that's on that same network.
So to disrupt IPIDEA, we led a synchronized
multi-pronged takedown.
We started with legal action, securing court orders to seize
and shutter the command domains controlling the proxy
traffic but we didn't keep the data to ourselves.
We shared technical intelligence on IPIDEA's SDKs
with law enforcement and platform providers to trigger
an industry-wide cleanup.
Finally, we used Google Play Protect, Android's built-in
security protection, to automatically warn users to
remove apps known to incorporate IPIDEA's SDKs
and block any future install attempts.
We believe our actions have caused significant degradation
of IPIDEA's proxy network and their business operations,
reducing the available pool of devices for the proxy
operators by millions and disrupting a tool used by
hundreds of threat actors.
In a single seven-day period in January of this year,
we actually observed over 550 individual threat groups
we tracked utilizing IP addresses that were tracked
as IPIDEA exit nodes to obfuscate their activities.
This includes groups from China, North Korea, Russia, and Iran.
By February 3rd, we saw meaningful and immediate impact.
For example, Okta had a 90% reduction in requests from
IPIDEA IP addresses, while Comcast had a 75% drop-off in
traffic from exit nodes.
We also directly observed the impact through adversaries
kind of whining about their infrastructure being taken down.
Here is the translation.
I feel like that's an advanced persistent tantrum, don't you?
And I like the sound of Guardians of the Galaxy.
It has a nice little ring to it.
But we should acknowledge that IPIDEA has been able to
rebuild some of their infrastructure following that,
but we are going back and doing even more disruption.
So this shows that disruption is just like security.
It's a process without a finish line, and it means
we need to continue to take action to disrupt adversaries
and their infrastructure.
It takes a community effort to truly knock these networks down.
The action that we took against IPIDEA is a serving
notice to this often overlooked corner of the threat
actor ecosystem that their actions don't go unnoticed,
and we will continue to disrupt them again and again.
Let's look at another example.
When we evaluate a target for disruption, we look for two
specific leverage points.
First, we look for points of failure.
Where can we disrupt to cause the most immediate damage to a
specific threat actor?
Second, we focus on pivot points, or places where a
single action can have scaled impact across multiple
actors at once.
Now, we found such a pivot point in the
certificate reseller market.
We identified a specific actor, a certificate reseller,
who is operating an industrial-scale automated
business, providing a streamlined pipeline for
threat actors to launder their malware and
make it appear legitimate.
So the single reseller was a primary source of trust for a
massive range of disparate threat groups,
acting as automated gatekeeper for malicious
activity across the web.
So to disrupt this operation, we coordinated directly with
certificate authorities, or CAs, to initiate a mass revocation
of compromised certificates.
By sharing specific TTPs, we didn't just kick actors off
of these platforms, we gave the CAs the telemetry
needed to sharpen their future detection.
Now, our investigation uncovered over 100 malicious
certificates tied to the single operation.
Now, the impact was immediate.
We stripped away their enterprise-grade legitimacy,
forcing them to pivot to individual
validation certificates.
Now, because these are reserved for personal projects,
they are largely untrusted by modern operating
systems and security tools.
So by providing actionable intelligence to the CA,
we successfully amplified our impact across an entire
network of actors towards less trustworthy credentials.
So within 10 weeks, we saw these actors migrate to a
far less sophisticated service, one that relies
on shared certificates.
This is a win for defense.
Shared certificates are significantly easier for us
to detect, track, and revoke at scale.
Now, active defense also means maintaining the integrity
of our own platforms.
GRIDTIDE is a prime example of why this matters.
We worked with our partners, and you know who you are, partners.
Thank you so much.
Thank you so much for working with us.
We worked with our partners to disrupt a
global espionage campaign targeting telecommunications
and government organizations in dozens of
nations across four continents.
The actor is a suspected PRC-nexus cyber espionage group,
that we have tracked since 2017 and had confirmed
intrusions in 42 countries when their disruption was executed.
The actor sought to exploit the trust and reliability of
Google's ecosystem, abusing Google Cloud for their heavy
lifting and Google Sheets for their stealthy mechanism
of command and control.
By leveraging legitimate services, they aim to blend
into normal enterprise traffic, making traditional
detection incredibly difficult.
Now, our response was designed to create
maximum operational friction.
We didn't just block their access;
we dismantled their environment.
We terminated all Google Cloud projects controlled by
the attacker, effectively severing persistent access
to environments that were compromised by the
novel GRIDTIDE backdoor.
We blinded their command and control by disabling and
revoking access to Google Sheets and their Google Cloud
accounts that they abused to hide in plain sight.
We also released a comprehensive set of IOCs to
the global community and deployed tailored signatures
to intercept related malware to ensure they
couldn't simply migrate these tactics elsewhere.
But perhaps most importantly, in collaboration with partners,
we identified and disabled all known infrastructure.
This included the sinkholing of both current and historical
domains to further dismantle the group's reach.
Now, these intrusions took this adversary years to build.
By stripping away their underlying environment,
we have ensured these operations cannot
be easily reestablished.
Now, we expect this actor will work hard to reestablish
their global footprint, but we are not going to make
it easy for them.
The same active defense philosophy we apply to proxy
networks and certificate resellers is now being applied
to the most important frontier of all: artificial intelligence.
So as adversaries adopt AI, we have a unique opportunity to
disrupt them at the source.
As a major provider, we take this responsibility seriously,
and we use four key levers to stay ahead.
The first is we disable malicious infrastructure, just
like we did with GRIDTIDE.
If you use our tools to facilitate an attack, you lose
access to those tools.
We proactively disable the projects, the accounts,
and assets of known bad actors.
We also harden our AI models and classifiers.
We operate a continuous feedback loop for Gemini and
for other AI models.
And by directly feeding the threat intelligence
into product development, our models learn to recognize
and refuse malicious requests before an attack
can even be generated.
Automating vulnerability hunting and patching
also disrupt adversaries.
We are moving from manual patching to AI-driven hunting.
Tools like Big Sleep are already discovering zero days
before they can be exploited while CodeMender is using Gemini
to automatically fix critical vulnerabilities in
the code itself.
And finally, we developed advanced defenses
and threat models.
Our teams at Google DeepMind are building
specialized defenses for generative AI and deploying
active monitoring across our entire ecosystem to
identify misuse in real time.
We are not going to wait for the AI-powered attack to happen.
We are using AI to make the entire ecosystem
inherently more secure.
Now, all of these efforts point to a single conclusion.
For disruption to work, we must activate as an industry.
This starts with building resilience.
Every disruption has to feed intelligence back into
our defenses, making the entire ecosystem more hostile
to future abuse.
We want to ensure that once a tactic is burned,
that it stays burned.
Now, this leads us to systemic protection.
We are moving beyond the era of cleanup.
By using intelligence to build new and native protections,
we aren't just kicking bad guys off platforms, we are
fixing the root causes to make it harder for them to
ever get back in.
For this to work, we need a whole-of-community approach.
This isn't just a job for tech giants.
Small and medium-sized enterprises are equally vital
to this mission, and we have to embrace a
flexible partnership model that prioritizes the most
effective collaborators for each specific threat.
And when we align this way, we do more than just
improve our metrics.
We create a new status quo, moving from merely
counting threats to actually countering them.
And we have a historic opportunity to shift the
narrative of cyber defense, once from a common and constant
retreat to one of collective action.
This means moving past competition
towards radical partnership.
I'm asking you to join us in making disruption
an industry-wide movement.
These partnerships between law enforcement, tech providers of
all sizes, and defenders on the front lines are the only
way to build true global resilience.
Together, we can finally break this 'Whack-a-mole' cycle.
By dismantling entire networks instead of chasing
individual indicators, we prove to our stakeholders and
to the public that defense actually works.
The vision is clear.
We have the intelligence.
Now, let's use it to tip the scales.
Together, let's transform fragmented defense into a
formidable, proactive force that leaves no place for bad
actors to hide.
Thank you so much.
